newsitem.title: UK: LME base metals consolidate, activity lacklustre.
newsitem.headline: LME base metals consolidate, activity lacklustre.

text.p: Copper failed to muster much excitement in a sluggish midday session on Wednesday, coming off early highs, and traders said the market was consolidating after recent price volatility.
Most of the other base metals on the London Metal Exchange (LME) similarly ended the morning kerb little changed after making a stab at slightly firmer levels in early trading.

Copper prices finished a quiet midday session at $2,279 per tonne, down $2 from Tuesday's kerb close and at the day's low. Prices came off an early high above $2,290, and cash to threes backwardation was barely wider at $36/$37.

"Some commission house buying came in during the pre-market to try to drum up some interest, but there's been no follow through. It's very quiet and barely traded in the first ring," a trader said. "I don't think we're going to see $2,300 for a while."
Another trader noted that copper's fund sell-off last week and subsequent bounce from $2,245 signalled a forthcoming consolidation period.
"Now it's going to take a breather and try to build a base before moving higher," he said, citing positive fundamentals for a bullish longer-term outlook.
Recent LME stock declines, including a drop of 1,100 tonnes on Wednesday, were helping to underpin the market, traders noted.
Dealers were less optimistic in the near term for aluminium, which they said was likely to test the downside in the near term, with this year's low around $1,535 as the number to watch.
However, aluminium finished the kerb slightly firmer at $1,560, up $5, although it ran into trouble during a bid to extend the gains.
Nickel made an early push above the important $7,400 level, but failed to hold above it and succumbed to selling pressure.
It settled at $7,370, compared to $7,390 on Tuesday.
Zinc and lead struggled to make any headway on the upside, despite Tuesday's positive closes.
Lead was $2 lower at $643 without approaching key resistance at $650.
Zinc was also $2 down at $1,257, despite a stock decline of 1,900 tonnes.

"The market's confidence, having been hit following the recent tecnical fund selling, has to an extent started to ignore the overall bullish fundamentals, which are ever supportive of higher prices," brokers Rudolf Wolff said of zinc in a report.
Tin was quiet and steady at $5,760, while alloy was indicated at $1,455/60, versus $1,450/55.
